items.title: L13: What Strengths questions look for at senior grades
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: Success Profiles define Strengths as the things a person does regularly, does well and enjoys, so that they perform at their best. Strengths questions are usually asked at interview, and sometimes in application forms or video interviews, and they are short and quick. A typical set includes questions such as 'What do you enjoy most about leading others?', 'Which tasks give you energy?' or 'Would you rather finish a task thoroughly or move quickly to the next?'. Interviewers usually listen for energy, speed of response and real enthusiasm, not for polished evidence. This is different from Behaviour questions, which ask for a past example described in detail and scored against the stated level. At senior grades the Strengths asked are often those the role needs, such as enjoying working with ambiguity, building networks or coaching others, and you are not told which Strengths are being tested beyond a general list in the advert. Candidates sometimes try to guess the 'right' answer, which can backfire: panels notice hesitation and rehearsed phrasing, and a candidate who claims to love detailed analysis may be asked a follow-up about it that exposes the claim. The better preparation is to reflect on what you genuinely enjoy and do well at work, then be ready to give a short honest answer with an example if asked. It also helps to read the advert and consider which Strengths it implies, and to be honest where a role may not suit you. Being open about preferences is not a weakness: the Strengths approach is designed to match people to roles in which they will perform well. Weak responses are long, hedged, or merely repeat the question.

questions.prompt: Which description matches how Success Profiles define Strengths?

options.text: Technical qualifications gained through study
Things you do regularly, do well and enjoy, which help you perform at your best
The tasks listed in your current job description, together with the targets set in your annual objectives
The Behaviours you find easiest to evidence

questions.hint: Strengths are about enjoyment plus performance.

questions.prompt: What are interviewers usually listening for in answers to Strengths questions?

options.text: A detailed account of an example scored against a level
Energy, spontaneity and real enthusiasm shown in short answers
Familiar phrases drawn from the advert's wording, repeated with confidence and polish
Evidence of formal qualifications and training

questions.hint: Strengths answers are quick and natural.

questions.prompt: A candidate tries to guess the 'right' Strength and claims to love detailed analysis. What is the main risk?

options.text: The panel will give extra marks because the answer appears to match the job closely
The panel will treat it as a Technical claim
A follow-up question about it can expose that the claim is not genuine
The answer will be too long to score

questions.prompt: Which preparation is most useful for Strengths questions?

options.text: Memorising a standard answer to each possible question so that delivery is smooth and fluent
Reading other candidates' answers to similar questions
Drafting a long written account of each Strength
Reflecting honestly on what you enjoy and do well, with a short example ready

questions.prompt: How do Strengths questions differ from Behaviour questions in the way they are scored?

options.text: Strengths are scored against the level in the advert, while Behaviours are scored on the enthusiasm shown in the reply
Both are scored on the length of the answer
Strengths are judged on the spontaneity and energy of the response, Behaviours on detailed evidence against a level
Both are scored only on whether the answer is accurate

questions.prompt: Why can saying a role may not suit a particular preference be acceptable?

options.text: It shows lack of commitment to the application and is likely to count against the candidate
It is treated as a weakness by every panel
The approach aims to match people to roles where they will perform well
It means the candidate has misread the advert

questions.prompt: Which response is typical of a weak answer to a Strengths question?

options.text: Short, direct and followed by a brief example that shows real interest in the work
Long, hedged, and mostly repeating the question back to the panel
Clear about what gives the candidate energy
Honest about a task the candidate dislikes

questions.prompt: Which Strength is most likely to be tested for a senior role that involves frequent change?

options.text: Enjoying repetitive checking of routine records where little ever changes from week to week
Enjoying working with ambiguity and shifting priorities
Enjoying work that never involves other people
Enjoying tasks where the steps are always the same

questions.hint: The role's demands shape the Strengths.

questions.prompt: The advert lists Strengths in general terms only. What is the sensible step?

options.text: Ask the panel before the interview exactly which Strengths questions they will use and in what order
Prepare only for Behaviour questions
Consider which Strengths the role implies and reflect on your own honestly
Assume Strengths will not be used at interview

questions.prompt: A candidate pauses for a long time before each Strengths answer. What impression might this give?

options.text: Strong analytical thinking and care over each answer, which panels reward at senior grades
Respect for the panel's questions
Rehearsed or uncertain responses, which can suggest the answers are not natural
A preference for detail that suits senior roles

questions.hint: Hesitation can signal a lack of genuine preference.

items.title: L13: Telling a Strengths question from a Behaviours question
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: Candidates sometimes answer the wrong kind of question. A Behaviour question asks for a past example: 'Tell us about a time when you had to persuade a sceptical senior colleague.' The assessor expects a structured account with your actions and a result, and scores it against the level in the advert. A Strengths question asks about preference or tendency: 'What do you enjoy most about bringing different people together?' or 'Do you prefer to plan carefully or to start work and adapt?' The assessor expects a quick, natural answer. Giving a long STAR story to a Strengths question is a common mistake: it can sound rehearsed and may lose the energy that panels look for. The opposite mistake is answering a Behaviour question with a general statement of preference, such as 'I always enjoy persuading people', which gives no evidence to score. A simple rule is that questions starting 'Tell us about a time' or 'Give us an example' are Behaviour questions, and those beginning 'What do you enjoy', 'How do you prefer' or offering a choice between two ways of working are Strengths questions. Some questions blend the two, such as 'What did you enjoy most about leading that project?' following a Behaviour answer; treat the second half as a Strengths question and answer it more briefly. At senior grades panels often ask both in one interview, and sometimes ask follow-ups on a Strengths answer to test whether it is genuine. A short example in a Strengths answer is acceptable, as long as it supports the answer and does not take over. Watch the time: a Strengths question is usually answered in well under a minute, and the aim is to give a clear answer and stop, not to fill the time.

questions.prompt: Which question is a Behaviour question?

options.text: What do you enjoy most about bringing people together?
Tell us about a time you persuaded a sceptical senior colleague
Do you prefer to plan carefully or to adapt as you go?
Which parts of a typical week give you energy, and which drain it?

questions.hint: It asks for a past example.

questions.prompt: Which question is a Strengths question?

options.text: Give us an example of a decision you made with limited information and little time
Describe how you handled a conflict in your team
Tell us about a time you led a change
Would you rather finish a task thoroughly or move quickly to the next?

questions.prompt: What is the main drawback of giving a long STAR story to a Strengths question?

options.text: It will be scored against the wrong grade level because the answer is too detailed
It takes the candidate over the word limit
It is treated as an overclaim
It can sound rehearsed and lose the natural energy the panel looks for

questions.prompt: A candidate answers a Behaviour question with 'I always enjoy persuading people.' What is missing?

options.text: A longer description of the candidate's feelings about persuading people at work
A reference to the advert's wording
A statement of how many people were persuaded
A specific past example with actions and a result that can be scored

questions.prompt: After a Behaviour answer the panel asks 'What did you enjoy most about leading that project?' How should the candidate treat it?

options.text: As a request for a second full STAR example, covering situation and result
As a Technical question about project methods
As a sign that the first answer was unclear
As a short Strengths-style question, answered briefly and naturally

questions.hint: Switch to a brief natural answer.

questions.prompt: Which opening words most reliably signal a Behaviour question?

options.text: Tell us about a time when
What do you most enjoy about
How do you prefer to
Which of these two do you

questions.prompt: How far can a short example be used in a Strengths answer?

options.text: It is never allowed in a Strengths answer, since Strengths are only matters of preference
It is required in every Strengths answer
It is allowed only for senior roles
It is allowed if it supports the answer and does not take over

questions.prompt: Why might panels ask a follow-up on a Strengths answer?

options.text: To give the candidate a second chance to write a statement
To test whether the preference is genuine and consistent
To check the answer against the advert's Technical requirement
To move the candidate to a Behaviour question

questions.prompt: A Strengths answer typically takes how long, in general terms?

options.text: Well under a minute, ending when the point is made
About five minutes, to cover situation, action and result
As long as the candidate wants, since there is no time guide
About ten minutes, matching a Behaviour question

questions.prompt: In a senior interview that includes both types, what is a sensible plan?

options.text: Use a STAR structure for every question
Recognise each question's type and answer in the matching style
Give brief preferences for every question, including those that ask for a past example
Ask the panel to say in advance which type is coming

items.title: L13: Ability tests at senior grades
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: Success Profiles describe Ability as the aptitude or potential to perform in a role, and in practice it is usually assessed by tests. Civil Service tests commonly include verbal, numerical and sometimes abstract or logical reasoning, and situational judgement tests (SJTs) that ask how you would handle a work scenario. At HEO and SEO level, recruiters often use an ability test as an early filter for a large field, and a common feature is a cut-off: candidates who do not reach the pass mark are not read further. Tests are timed and take place online, sometimes supervised remotely. For many promotion campaigns the advert states the type and the date of the test, so preparation can be planned. Typical preparation is to practise sample questions in the same format, learn to manage time rather than aim to answer every question, and be familiar with basic calculations, such as percentages, ratios and reading tables. Some employers publish examples of the question types. Reasonable adjustments, for example extra time for a disability or condition, can be requested by contacting the recruitment team before the test. Because the test is an early filter, strong Behaviour statements will not be read if the cut-off is missed, so preparation time should be balanced. At senior grade, an e-tray or in-tray exercise may also be used, in which you handle a simulated inbox and prioritise, delegate and respond. In such exercises, assessors look for sound judgement, clear reasoning and attention to the stakeholders affected. A scenario-based SJT usually asks you to rank or choose actions; the best answers tend to follow the Civil Service Code and the values in the question, such as honesty, objectivity and fairness, rather than the quickest option. Keep your answers consistent with the role's grade.

questions.prompt: How do Success Profiles define Ability?

options.text: The experience built up in earlier posts
The technical skills needed for a specific job
The preferences you enjoy at work
The aptitude or potential to perform in a role

questions.prompt: Why does a cut-off score matter for a candidate with excellent Behaviour statements?

options.text: If the cut-off is missed, the statements are not read
The statements are marked down for lower scores
The cut-off applies only to the interview
The cut-off is waived for internal candidates who already work in the department

questions.hint: Early filters can end the application.

questions.prompt: Which preparation is typically useful for a timed numerical test?

options.text: Memorising past test questions word for word from the practice material available
Working on a long written statement
Practising sample questions in the same format and managing time
Learning the names of the assessors

questions.prompt: A candidate has a condition that makes timed tests harder. What should they do?

options.text: Wait until after the test to explain
Ask a colleague to take the test for them
Skip the test and rely on the quality of the written statement to carry the application
Contact the recruitment team before the test to request reasonable adjustments

questions.hint: Adjustments must be requested in advance.

questions.prompt: In a situational judgement test, which answer pattern usually fits best?

options.text: Actions that reflect Civil Service Code values such as honesty, objectivity and fairness
Actions that save the most time in the scenario and keep the workload of the team down
Actions that avoid involving any other person
Actions that match the candidate's usual habit

questions.prompt: What are assessors looking for in an e-tray exercise?

options.text: The largest number of messages answered in the time, whatever the quality of each reply
The longest replies to each message
Fast typing and consistent formatting
Sound judgement, clear reasoning and attention to the stakeholders affected

questions.prompt: Which statement about managing time in a test is accurate?

options.text: Aim for accuracy on as many questions as you can, not an attempt at every question
Always attempt every question in the time available, guessing wherever you are unsure of the answer
Spend most of the time on the first few questions
Stop as soon as one question seems hard

questions.prompt: Why should a candidate balance preparation time between tests and statements?

options.text: Because statements are not read at all
Because tests are worth more than the interview in the final score for the role
Because tests are optional
Because an early test can filter out a candidate before statements are read

questions.prompt: What does a numerical reasoning test usually involve at this level?

options.text: Writing a short report on a policy
Reading tables and graphs and doing calculations such as percentages and ratios
Advanced mathematics of a kind taught in a degree course in statistics or physics
Explaining a past example

questions.prompt: In an in-tray exercise, a request from a senior leader conflicts with a deadline from a partner. What is the best approach?

options.text: Always do what the senior leader asked first, since their instruction outranks any partner's request
Ignore both and wait for more detail
Weigh the impact, consider who is affected, then decide and explain your reasoning
Delegate both tasks without checking

items.title: L13: Technical skills and professional requirements
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: Technical skills in Success Profiles are the specific knowledge, qualifications or capabilities a role requires, and they are assessed against the stated requirement. At senior grades, Technical elements are common in professional roles, such as finance, legal, analysis, digital, commercial and project delivery. A requirement might be a professional qualification, membership of a professional body, a demonstrated capability using a tool or method, or knowledge of a legislative framework. Many professions in government have their own competence frameworks, and the advert may refer to them. Typical assessment includes checking a qualification at application or offer, a written exercise or technical interview, a case study, a presentation or a work sample. If a Technical requirement is stated as a minimum criterion, it must be met to proceed: a strong Behaviour statement cannot make up for a missing qualification. If the requirement is a skill rather than a qualification, evidence should show what you did, with what tool or method, at what level, and what it produced. For example, 'I built and maintained a model in Excel that forecast monthly demand within a margin the team agreed, and used it to change staffing' is more informative than 'I am skilled in Excel'. Technical evidence differs from Experience evidence: Technical skills show what you can do now, whereas Experience shows what you have done in earlier roles. Candidates sometimes treat a Technical requirement as a Behaviour and answer with a STAR story where a direct demonstration was wanted. Read how the advert says it will be assessed. Where a qualification is 'desirable' not 'essential', mention it, but do not rely on it for the sift. Ensure that any claim about technical competence is accurate, since it will be tested at assessment or in practice.

questions.prompt: How are Technical skills assessed, in general?

options.text: Against the stated requirement, such as a qualification or demonstrated skill
Against the grade level of the Behaviour wording
By the length of time in the current grade
By the panel's general impression of how confident the candidate seems with the subject

questions.prompt: A Technical requirement is stated as a minimum criterion and the candidate lacks it. What is the likely outcome?

options.text: The statement will be scored higher to compensate
The application cannot proceed however strong the Behaviour statement is
The panel will waive it for internal candidates who have shown strong potential in post
The requirement will be moved to the interview

questions.prompt: Which statement is the stronger Technical evidence?

options.text: I am skilled in Excel and use it every day
I built an Excel demand forecast the team agreed, and used it to change staffing
I have used Excel for many years across several of my roles and regularly show colleagues how to use it
I always check my spreadsheets carefully

questions.prompt: How does Technical differ from Experience in Success Profiles?

options.text: Technical covers what you have done in earlier roles, whereas Experience covers current abilities
Technical shows what you can do now, Experience what you have done in earlier roles
They are the same and used interchangeably
Technical is assessed only at interview

questions.prompt: Why can answering a Technical requirement with a STAR story be a mistake?

options.text: STAR stories are not allowed for Technical skills, which may be shown only by qualifications
The assessment may need a direct demonstration or check of the skill, not a story
STAR stories are always too long
Technical skills are never assessed in writing

questions.prompt: Which is a typical way to assess a Technical requirement?

options.text: A case study, work sample, technical interview or check of a qualification
A general personality questionnaire completed online, with results compared to the role profile
A short Strengths question
A reference from a friend

questions.prompt: A qualification is described as desirable. How should the candidate treat it?

options.text: Ignore it, since desirable criteria are never scored at the sift or the interview
Treat it as a minimum criterion
Mention it, but do not rely on it alone to pass the sift
Mention it only at interview

questions.prompt: Which professions in government commonly publish competence frameworks?

options.text: Only the legal profession, which is the sole profession with a published framework
Finance, analysis, digital, commercial and project delivery
Only the Diplomatic Service
None, since frameworks are for the private sector

questions.prompt: A candidate over-states their technical skill at application. What risk does this carry?

options.text: It will be scored as extra evidence
It will have no effect unless the panel includes a technical specialist who tests it
It can be exposed at assessment or in the job, harming the application and trust
It will be treated as a Strengths answer

questions.prompt: What details make a technical skill claim credible?

options.text: The number of years since training
The name of the course provider and the date on which the qualification was awarded
What was done, with what tool or method, at what level and with what result
A statement that colleagues rely on you

items.title: L13: Experience as an element at senior grades
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: Experience in Success Profiles means the knowledge and mastery gained from working in a role or profession. It is usually assessed from the application or CV, and sometimes at interview, and the advert says what is needed, such as experience of managing a budget, handling parliamentary business or working in a regulated environment. At senior grades, Experience requirements are often broader and tied to context: for instance, experience of leading change in a large organisation, working with ministers, or managing external suppliers. Experience differs from Behaviours: a Behaviour is demonstrated by a particular example against a level, whereas Experience is judged by whether you have worked in the relevant area for a sufficient period or at sufficient scope. Experience is also not the same as length of service: ten years in one routine job may offer less relevant experience than two in a role with a wide remit. Evidence should state what you did, the scale and the setting, not only job titles. Examples include: the size of budget you managed, whether you were accountable for it, the number of suppliers, or whether you ran a programme with external stakeholders. Where Experience comes from outside the Civil Service, such as a commercial, charity or military role, the advert may say that it counts, and the candidate should translate it into terms that an assessor understands, avoiding jargon. Experience from acting-up, secondments and loans is usually relevant and should be described with dates and scope. Be honest about the limits of Experience; claiming experience you lack is risky, since it can be checked by references and at interview. If you lack a stated area, consider whether related experience can be described accurately, and say how it compares.

questions.prompt: How is Experience in Success Profiles best described?

options.text: A specific example scored against a Behaviour level
A test of aptitude and potential to learn that is taken before the interview
The knowledge and mastery gained from working in a role or profession
A preference for certain kinds of work

questions.prompt: Why is length of service not the same as relevant Experience?

options.text: Length of service is never mentioned in applications
Longer service always gives more relevant experience, because the candidate has seen more of the work
Years in a routine job may offer less relevant experience than fewer years in a wide-ranging role
Experience is judged only by qualifications

questions.prompt: Which detail makes Experience evidence stronger?

options.text: The job title alone, since senior titles are reliable evidence of the experience held
The name of the line manager
The location of the post
The scale and setting, such as budget size and whether you were accountable for it

questions.prompt: A candidate has relevant experience from the voluntary sector. What should they do?

options.text: Leave it out because it is not Civil Service experience and assessors cannot compare it fairly
Describe it in sector jargon
Treat it as a Technical qualification
Check whether the advert allows it and describe it in terms an assessor understands

questions.prompt: How should acting-up or secondment experience be presented?

options.text: As a single line stating the title
With dates and scope, describing what the role covered
Only if the role was permanent, since temporary roles carry no weight with assessors
Only at interview

questions.prompt: What distinguishes Experience from a Behaviour example?

options.text: Experience is judged on the area and scope you have worked in, Behaviours on one example
Experience must be recent, Behaviours may be old
Experience is scored only at interview, whereas Behaviours are scored only at the sift stage
They are assessed in the same way

questions.prompt: A candidate lacks one stated area of Experience. What is the honest approach?

options.text: Describe related experience accurately and say how it compares
Claim the experience and be ready to discuss it
Ignore the requirement
Ask a colleague who has the experience to provide a reference stating that you share it

questions.prompt: Which Experience requirement is typical of a senior role?

options.text: Using the department's staff intranet and attending the regular all-staff briefings
Attending team meetings
Following written procedures
Leading change in a large organisation or working with ministers

questions.prompt: Where is Experience usually assessed?

options.text: From the application or CV, and sometimes at interview
Only through an online test taken before the application is read
Only through a presentation
Only from references

questions.prompt: Why is claiming experience you lack risky?

options.text: It can be checked by references and tested at interview
It is not scored at all
It results in an automatic extra mark

items.title: L13: How the Behaviours change at Grade 7
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: At Grade 7, the Behaviours usually describe leading a significant area of work with real autonomy, shaping rather than only delivering the direction, and influencing across organisational boundaries. As a general pattern, the step up from SEO is again about scope, independence and consequence. In Seeing the Big Picture, a Grade 7 is expected to take a longer view, understand how policy, delivery, finance and politics interact, and shape plans with a clear line of sight to government priorities. In Leadership, the emphasis moves towards setting a compelling direction, building leaders beneath you, and holding a unit together through uncertainty, ambiguity and external scrutiny. Examples may include leading a policy or operational area through a change in government priorities, managing a team after a serious incident, or taking forward a politically sensitive project. Assessors look for judgement in the way you carry authority: how you consulted, how you listened to challenge and how you made unpopular decisions well. Grade 7 candidates are expected to see their work in the context of the system, so evidence about connecting your area to others, and anticipating the effects of your decisions elsewhere, is relevant. Evidence at this level that stays inside a single team or a single project, however well delivered, is often below the grade. Equally, simply having a large budget or headcount is not evidence of the Behaviour; what matters is what you did with it. Use the advert's wording to check the level, and remember that these patterns are general, since departments describe grade expectations in their own way.

questions.prompt: Which three features mark the step up from SEO to Grade 7 as a general pattern?

options.text: Scope, independence and consequence
Length of service, salary and team size
Age, qualifications and title
Reporting lines, location and budget

questions.hint: The step up is in breadth, autonomy and consequence.

questions.prompt: Which example best shows Seeing the Big Picture at Grade 7?

options.text: Explaining the team's priorities clearly to every member of staff and checking they each understood their part
Following the department's annual plan
Reshaping an area's plan after government priorities changed, linking policy, delivery and finance
Reporting on the team's current projects

questions.prompt: What does Leadership at Grade 7 emphasise?

options.text: Setting a compelling direction, building leaders below you and steadying a unit through uncertainty
Supervising individual tasks closely and approving every piece of work before it goes out of the unit
Monitoring attendance and leave
Preparing the weekly team meeting

questions.prompt: A candidate cites a large headcount and budget only. How would an assessor see this?

options.text: As strong evidence of the Behaviour because the scale of the responsibility is so large at this grade
As evidence of Delivering at Pace
As evidence of Managing a Quality Service
As description of the post, not evidence of the Behaviour, since what the candidate did is missing

questions.prompt: Which indicates that evidence is below Grade 7?

options.text: It stays inside a single team or project, however well delivered
It involves a politically sensitive project
It involves challenge from other parts of government and a deadline set by ministers
It affects several teams

questions.prompt: What do assessors look for in how a Grade 7 carries authority?

options.text: Making every decision alone, to show clear and decisive ownership of the result
Consulting well, listening to challenge and making unpopular decisions with care
Avoiding difficult decisions
Passing decisions upward

questions.prompt: Why is it important to see work in the context of the system at Grade 7?

options.text: Because assessors reward detailed knowledge of every other department's structure
Because system knowledge is the only Behaviour assessed
Because Grade 7 is a policy grade only
Decisions in one area affect others, and anticipating that shows senior judgement

questions.prompt: Which statement about grade patterns is the most careful?

options.text: They are exact, fixed national thresholds that every department must apply in its adverts
They are the same for every Behaviour
They are general, since departments describe grade expectations in their own way
They apply only to the Senior Civil Service

questions.prompt: How should a candidate check the level pitched in the advert?

options.text: Read the advert's wording for each Behaviour and compare with the example's scope
Assume the level from the salary
Ask a colleague who works in the department
Look at last year's advert for a different role in the same department as a comparison

questions.prompt: A Grade 7 example describes leading a team through a serious incident. Which detail would strengthen it?

options.text: The date and time of the incident
The number of staff in the department
The titles and grades of the people who wrote the report on the incident afterwards
What was said and decided, how people were supported, and what lasting change followed

items.title: L13: Decisions and change at Grade 7
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: For Making Effective Decisions at Grade 7, the decision typically carries significant consequences for services, public money or policy, and may involve ministers, other departments or the public. Assessors usually expect you to show how you handled complexity: conflicting evidence, risk to delivery, value for money and legal considerations. A strong example describes the options, the criteria and the reasoning, who was consulted and why, and how you decided what to take to ministers and what to decide yourself. Decisions at this level are often made when the evidence is incomplete and the clock is running; assessors look for how you handled that tension rather than waiting for certainty. They also look for ownership: what you did when the decision proved wrong or politically unwelcome. Changing and Improving at Grade 7 usually involves leading change that spans a service or policy area, with design, sponsorship, risk and benefits all in view. Typical evidence includes building a case with data, bringing different parties along, testing in a controlled way and learning from early results, then scaling. At this level, an assessor will often be alert to the difference between leading the change and administrating it. They may also look for evidence that you stopped or reshaped work that was not working, and for how you handled the effect on staff and service users. Weak examples rely on describing a programme's overall results without your own decisions, and strong ones show the difficult choices you made. Where legal advice, finance advice or analytical input shaped the decision, mention how you used it, as a senior decision-maker is expected to draw on specialists without handing the judgement to them.

questions.prompt: Which feature best marks a Grade 7 decision example?

options.text: Significant consequences for services, public money or policy, made with incomplete evidence
A decision between two equal options in a small team where nothing much turns on the choice
A decision with a clearly correct answer
A decision made by a manager and communicated

questions.prompt: What does 'handling the tension' of incomplete evidence mean?

options.text: Delaying the decision until all of the evidence is available, whatever the cost in time
Passing the decision to a minister
Choosing the first option offered
Deciding at the right moment without waiting for certainty, while managing the risk

questions.prompt: A decision proved politically unwelcome. What would assessors value in the answer?

options.text: A statement that the decision was correct at the time, given what was known then
Ownership: what the candidate did next and how they handled the consequences
Evidence that others agreed with it
An explanation that the minister decided

questions.prompt: What difference might an assessor look for between leading and administrating a change?

options.text: Whether the candidate attended every meeting about the change and took the notes
Whether the change was completed on time
Whether the candidate produced the plan document
Whether the candidate made the key design, sponsorship and risk decisions

questions.prompt: Why mention how specialist advice was used in a decision?

options.text: Specialist advice must always be followed, because specialists carry the responsibility
A senior decision-maker draws on specialists without handing the judgement to them
Specialists are the real decision-makers
Specialist advice is irrelevant at Grade 7

questions.prompt: Which element best shows change learned from early results?

options.text: Rolling out in full on the first day so that all users receive the benefits at once
Waiting for the sponsor to review it
Testing in a controlled way, learning from the results and adjusting before scaling
Repeating the same plan for a second year

questions.prompt: Which weak pattern appears when describing a programme?

options.text: Describing the choices made under pressure and the reasons given for each one
Describing the risks that were managed
Describing how the effect on staff was handled
Describing the overall results without saying what the candidate decided

questions.prompt: Which is the best sign of stopping or reshaping work that was not working?

options.text: Continuing with the plan to avoid criticism from sponsors and others who had backed it
Reviewing results, deciding to stop a strand and explaining why to those affected
Leaving the work to wind down unnoticed
Moving staff without telling them

questions.prompt: Which consideration is typical in a Grade 7 decision about public money?

options.text: The preference of the sponsor's private office for the quickest possible visible result
The shortest route to a quick and visible result for the minister
The enjoyment of the team and their preference for the least change
Value for money, risk to delivery, legal considerations and the interests of users

questions.prompt: What should you include about who was consulted?

options.text: Why those people were chosen and how their views affected the decision
A full list of names with their grades and the dates on which they were consulted
Only the senior people consulted
Only those who agreed with the plan

items.title: L13: Influence and partnerships at Grade 7
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: Communicating and Influencing at Grade 7 usually involves shaping decisions and opinions at a senior level, often in settings where you lack authority: ministers' offices, other departments, external bodies, the media and the public. A typical evidence pattern is advising ministers on a sensitive matter, negotiating with another department about funding or responsibilities, presenting a case at a board or to a parliamentary committee, or handling an external audience that is hostile. Assessors expect clarity, a considered choice of channel, and awareness of what each party needs. Because Civil Service impartiality applies, you should be able to show that advice to ministers was honest, evidence-based and not shaded to please, and that once a decision was made, you implemented it fully even if you had advised otherwise. Working Together at Grade 7 typically means building and sustaining relationships across a system: with other departments, arm's-length bodies, local government, suppliers and delivery partners. Evidence includes handling genuine conflicts of interest between parties, creating joint governance that actually works, and sharing credit generously. Often, the test is whether partners would say you made the partnership easier or harder. A frequent weakness is describing an alliance of friendly bodies with no difficulty. Another is a story in which the candidate's own department prevailed but damaged the long-term relationship. Think also about inclusion at system level, for example how you involved communities affected by a policy, or ensured that groups with less power were heard. Where a single story could fit either Behaviour, decide which action is central: persuading and shaping goes with Communicating and Influencing, whereas building and maintaining a joint way of working goes with Working Together.

questions.prompt: Which setting is most typical of Grade 7 Communicating and Influencing?

options.text: Advising ministers or negotiating with another department without authority over them
Briefing your own team each week on progress against the plan and answering their questions
Writing minutes of a team meeting
Following a communications plan written by others and approved by the press office, then reporting results back to them

questions.prompt: What does impartiality imply for advice to ministers?

options.text: It should always agree with the minister
It should be honest and evidence-based, and decisions implemented fully once made
It should avoid contentious evidence so that ministers are not put in an awkward position
It should be given only in writing

questions.prompt: Which test applies to a Working Together example at Grade 7?

options.text: Whether the meetings ran on time
Whether the candidate chaired the partnership board throughout the whole programme
Whether partners would say you made the partnership easier or harder
Whether the partners were senior to the candidate

questions.prompt: Why is an alliance of friendly bodies with no difficulty a weak example?

options.text: It shows nothing of how conflict between parties was handled
It is too short to score
It is not allowed at Grade 7, where partnerships must involve conflict to be valid
It uses too many partners

questions.prompt: What is the weakness in a story where the candidate's department prevailed but the relationship was damaged?

options.text: It shows that the candidate lost the argument and had to accept the other department's terms
It shows too much collaboration with partners at the expense of the department
It cannot be scored
It shows short-term success at the expense of the long-term working relationship

questions.prompt: A candidate's answer is mostly about persuading a director to approve a plan. Which Behaviour is it likely to fit best?

options.text: Working Together
Seeing the Big Picture
Communicating and Influencing
Delivering at Pace

questions.prompt: Which action shows system-level inclusion?

options.text: Involving communities affected by a policy and making sure less powerful groups were heard
Consulting only the largest and best-organised stakeholders so that the process stays manageable
Informing affected groups clearly after the decision has been taken and explaining the reasons
Limiting input to senior officials in the partner bodies, who can commit their organisations

questions.prompt: How should a candidate describe implementing a decision they advised against?

options.text: Describe how they quietly delayed it until the minister reconsidered, to protect the service
Show they carried it out fully and professionally, having given their advice honestly
Leave out the fact that they advised against it, so that the account shows full commitment
Say the decision was theirs, since they carried it out and answered for the result

questions.prompt: Which is a sign of generous credit-sharing?

options.text: Presenting the success as your department's, since it carried the main risk and the cost
Mentioning partners only in private thank-you messages once the work is finished and closed
Thanking the sponsor alone in the final report, as the person accountable for the programme
Naming partners' contributions publicly and in the formal record

questions.prompt: What does a considered choice of channel show?

options.text: A preference for formal documents in all circumstances, to leave a clear audit trail
That the candidate avoids meetings and prefers to work in writing wherever possible
Awareness of what each audience needs and how they will best take in the message
That the candidate has ample time to prepare a different version for each audience

items.title: L13: People, quality and delivery at Grade 7
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: At Grade 7, Developing Self and Others typically concerns building a leadership pipeline, shaping culture, and handling the hardest people issues with fairness. Evidence includes coaching people who are themselves managers, ensuring that talent is identified and promoted fairly, managing a difficult performance case, and learning from senior peers or critical feedback. Self-development at this level is judged by self-awareness and change, such as asking for challenging feedback from those you lead and altering how you work. Managing a Quality Service at Grade 7 concerns the quality, risk and resilience of a significant service, often under external scrutiny from audit bodies, Parliament or the public. Typical evidence includes setting a quality framework, responding to an audit or review, reporting honestly on risk, or building resilience after a failure. Assessors look for the use of reliable management information, openness about failure, and attention to users, including vulnerable ones. Delivering at Pace at Grade 7 usually concerns delivery of a portfolio or a high-profile project against political and financial constraints, with the candidate making trade-offs, managing dependencies and maintaining confidence with sponsors and ministers. The key test is whether the candidate made explicit choices: what to prioritise, what to stop, what to accept as a risk, and how to protect the team. Common weaknesses include describing delivery as a series of heroics, ignoring quality in the pursuit of pace, and presenting rosy progress reports. A strong answer shows how the candidate raised problems early, set realistic expectations and rebuilt confidence after a setback. Because the three Behaviours overlap, check that your example makes the central action clear and does not try to prove everything.

questions.prompt: What does Developing Self and Others typically emphasise at Grade 7?

options.text: Delivering induction training to new starters and keeping a record of those who attended
Building a leadership pipeline, shaping culture and handling hard people issues fairly
Recording attendance at training sessions and reporting completion rates to senior leaders
Completing your own annual objectives and receiving a good performance marking each year

questions.prompt: How is self-development judged at this level?

options.text: By the number of courses completed and the qualifications gained in the last few years
By self-awareness and change, such as seeking challenging feedback and altering how you work
By the date of the last appraisal and the marking that the candidate was given in it
By the opinions of senior colleagues outside the candidate's line, gathered informally

questions.prompt: Which is a typical source of external scrutiny for a significant service?

options.text: Audit bodies, parliamentary committees or the public
A single customer's compliment sent to the team
The team's own internal review of its monthly results
A single customer's letter of complaint about a delay

questions.prompt: What would assessors value in reporting on a quality failure?

options.text: A defence that the failure was unavoidable given the resources and the timescale the service had
A statement that nobody was individually responsible, since the cause was a systemic one
A focus on speed of repair alone, with little said about causes or the people affected
Openness, reliable management information and attention to users, including vulnerable ones

questions.prompt: What is the key test of delivering a portfolio at Grade 7?

options.text: Whether the candidate made explicit choices about priorities, stops and accepted risks
Whether every project in the portfolio was finished on the original date set at the start
Whether the candidate worked long hours and showed commitment throughout the programme
Whether the sponsor was happy with progress at each of the regular review meetings

questions.prompt: Which pattern is a weakness in a delivery story?

options.text: Showing the risks that were raised early and the actions that followed from them
Showing the plan changed after a review of progress with the sponsor in the middle of the work
Describing delivery as a series of heroics by the candidate, with little about how the work was planned or controlled
Showing how the team was protected from unreasonable demands as the deadline came closer

questions.prompt: What does raising problems early and resetting expectations show?

options.text: That the project was badly planned and the candidate is looking to pass the blame
That the sponsor was unhelpful and had set targets that nobody could meet
Honest control of delivery and a way to rebuild confidence
That the candidate avoided accountability by moving the problem to the sponsor's desk

questions.prompt: Why check that an example makes the central action clear?

options.text: Because assessors always prefer short answers that do not try to cover several Behaviours
Because only one Behaviour is allowed per statement, however many the advert lists
Because Behaviours overlap and trying to prove everything dilutes the evidence
Because the word limit forbids detail about a second Behaviour in the same example

questions.prompt: Which example best shows building a leadership pipeline?

options.text: Training all staff in the same leadership course so that each person gets equal opportunity
Identifying potential in managers, giving stretch roles and sponsoring them fairly
Keeping the best people in their current roles so that the service stays stable and reliable
Recruiting externally for every senior post so that fresh ideas keep coming into the area

questions.prompt: How should a candidate handle a difficult performance case in a statement?

options.text: Describe it in detail including the personal circumstances that explained the performance
Leave out the process followed and state only the outcome that was reached for the individual
Describe it in general terms, showing fair process and their own actions without private detail
State that the person was dismissed and describe the reasons given to the senior team

items.title: L13: Matching examples to grade: HEO, SEO or Grade 7?
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: A good test of understanding is to read an example and place it at a grade. Consider the following three versions of a Changing and Improving example. Version one: 'I noticed that our complaints form had unclear questions, redesigned it and shared the new version with my team, and the number of incomplete forms fell.' This is a sound EO-level example: the change is small, owned by the candidate and measured. Version two: 'I led a review of how three teams handled complaints, found that duplicated checks caused delay, designed a single process with team leaders, piloted it, and reduced the average time to resolve complaints by a fifth.' This is typical HEO, because the scope crosses teams, the candidate led, and the benefit was measured. Version three: 'I was asked by the director to lead a change to how a service handled complaints across four locations, including a supplier. I built the case with data on cost and user experience, negotiated the changes with the supplier and unions, led the managers through the transition, and reported benefits and risks to the board, stopping one element that was not working.' This fits SEO and above, because of scope, stakeholders, formal governance and the stopping decision. An example moves towards Grade 7 when it includes a wider system effect, such as shaping a policy, working across departments or meeting ministerial priorities. Notice that in none of the versions are the verbs the main difference; the difference is in who was affected, who decided, and how complex the interests were. When pitching a promotion, ensure at least one example is at the target grade, and be ready to show how your current role gives you that scope, even without the title.

questions.prompt: Version one redesigns a form for the team and measures fewer incomplete forms. Which grade pattern does it best fit?

options.text: SEO level, because it involved measuring a result
Grade 7 level, because the change was measured and owned by the candidate
Entry AA level, because it concerned only a form
EO level, with small scope, owned by the candidate and measured

questions.prompt: Version two reviews complaints across three teams and cuts resolution time by a fifth. Which grade pattern does it best fit?

options.text: EO level, because the candidate carried out a review of existing practice
HEO level, because it crosses teams, is led by the candidate and is measured
Grade 7 level, because the result was measured and the time saved was large
AO level, because the complaints process is a routine and administrative one

questions.prompt: What features move version three to SEO or above?

options.text: Wider scope, a supplier and unions, formal governance and a decision to stop an element
The use of the word led and other strong action verbs in the first sentence
A longer sentence structure with more formal vocabulary
The mention of data on cost and user experience used in the case

questions.prompt: What would move an example towards Grade 7?

options.text: A wider system effect such as shaping policy, working across departments or meeting ministerial priorities
Adding more figures and percentages to every sentence of the example to show scale
Using more senior-sounding verbs such as shaped, drove and championed throughout the example
Working longer hours on the project than other members of the team did

questions.prompt: Which factors mainly differentiate the versions?

options.text: The choice of verbs such as led, designed and negotiated in each version
Who was affected, who decided and how complex the interests were
The length of the statement and the number of figures quoted in it
The year the work was done and the size of the department concerned

questions.prompt: Why should a promotion candidate include at least one example at the target grade?

options.text: It is required by the Civil Service Code for any application for promotion
It replaces the need for examples at other grades elsewhere in the application
It shows they can already operate at that scope
It guarantees a pass at the sift, since assessors score only the highest-grade example

questions.prompt: A candidate lacks the title but has the scope in their current role. What should they do?

options.text: Describe the scope and responsibility actually held, honestly
Claim the title held by the person you worked for, as the scope was effectively the same
Avoid mentioning the role and describe only the individual projects that were led
Describe the manager's scope and explain that you worked closely with them on it

questions.prompt: A version says 'I was asked by the director to lead the change', then describes designing it. How should an assessor treat the instruction?

options.text: Not as a problem in itself, since independence lies in what the candidate then decided
As low independence, because any instruction from a director removes the candidate's ownership
As a likely overclaim, because directors do not ask staff of that grade to lead changes of that size
As evidence that the director did the real design work and the candidate only administered it

questions.prompt: How should a candidate respond if the only available example is at EO level?

options.text: Inflate the EO example with senior language so that it reads at the target grade
Use it for every Behaviour, with a different emphasis each time to show breadth
Skip the Behaviour and write more about the other Behaviours where evidence is stronger
Look for a larger example, and if none, build the scope honestly from what they actually led

questions.prompt: What is the main danger of rewording an EO example in senior language?

options.text: It makes the statement shorter and removes the detail that a panel would like to see
It can overclaim and be exposed when the panel probes the real scope
It matches the advert too closely, so the panel suspects the candidate copied the wording
It reduces the number of verbs available for describing the candidate's own actions

items.title: L13: Lead Behaviours and weighting in senior campaigns
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: Many senior adverts name a few lead Behaviours, which are the ones assessed most heavily, and sometimes list other Behaviours that may be tested at interview. The advert normally states how each element is used at each stage: for example, an Ability test first, then a written statement on one or two lead Behaviours, then an interview covering the lead Behaviours, other Behaviours and Strengths. Where a lead Behaviour is listed, you should expect a full STAR example for it, and you may be asked for another example at interview. If an advert asks for a short personal statement, rather than separate Behaviour answers, it is worth mapping your examples to the Behaviours so the panel can find the evidence. The weight placed on elements differs by role, and the advert will say whether Experience or Technical skills are only a gateway or part of the score. A useful way to prepare is to build a grid: list the elements the advert assesses, the stage at which each is assessed and the evidence you will use, noting where an example is reused. A common mistake is to prepare strongly for the lead Behaviours and leave the others to chance, even though the interview may include them; a pair of short, good examples for each of the remaining Behaviours is a sensible target. Another mistake is to assume that the same Behaviours are lead in every promotion round: they change by role. Also check how the final decision is made, for example whether scores from different stages are added or whether each must be passed. If the advert is unclear, ask recruitment. Update the grid after every application and keep a record of what you submitted, so you stay consistent.

questions.prompt: What is a lead Behaviour?

options.text: One used only at the sift stage and set aside at the interview
One chosen by the candidate from the nine, because it suits their best examples
One that is listed in the advert but not assessed at any stage of the process
One assessed most heavily, usually requiring a full example

questions.prompt: If an advert asks for a personal statement, what is a useful approach?

options.text: Write a general account of your career, leaving the panel to find the Behaviours in it
Avoid naming Behaviours, since the panel will see them without being told
Map your examples to the Behaviours so the panel can find the evidence
Write only about the lead Behaviour, since the others will not be looked at

questions.prompt: What is a sensible target for non-lead Behaviours that may be tested at interview?

options.text: Light preparation only, since they are not the lead Behaviours
A pair of short, good examples prepared for each of them
One strong example reused for all of them with a different emphasis
A full-length written statement prepared for each of them

questions.prompt: What does a grid of elements, stages and evidence help show?

options.text: The date of each stage of the process and the person responsible for it
The panel members for each stage and the questions that each is likely to ask
Where gaps and reused examples are
The order of questions in the interview, so that answers can be rehearsed in sequence

questions.prompt: Why is it a mistake to assume the same lead Behaviours apply in every round?

options.text: They are fixed for each grade and identical in every department's adverts
They change by role, so the advert must be read each time
They are chosen by the applicant at the sift stage from among the nine listed
They do not matter once the sift has been passed, as the interview covers all nine

questions.prompt: What should a candidate check about how the final decision is made?

options.text: The panel members' names and grades, which are published in every Civil Service advert
The date of the offer and the starting salary for the successful candidate
The number of applicants and the proportion who are expected to reach the interview
Whether scores from stages are added or each stage must be passed

questions.prompt: A candidate receives an advert that is unclear about what is assessed. What is sensible?

options.text: Guess which elements will matter most and prepare mostly for those
Wait until the interview and ask the panel what each stage was intended to test
Ask the recruitment team before the closing date
Apply with a general statement and hope that the panel will map it to the elements

questions.prompt: Why keep a record of submitted statements?

options.text: To send to other departments as evidence that the candidate has applied for senior roles
To prove that the word count was met if the panel queries it
To stay consistent when asked to expand at interview
To submit again unchanged for the next round of the same competition

questions.prompt: What does it mean if Technical skills are 'a gateway'?

options.text: They must be met to proceed but do not add to the score
They count double in the final score for the successful candidate
They are assessed by the panel only at interview, by a general question
They are optional and only used to separate candidates with equal scores

questions.prompt: What is a sign that preparation is unbalanced?

options.text: A grid with no gaps, showing each element covered by at least one example
Several well-chosen examples for each Behaviour, kept separate and distinct
Strong lead examples but nothing ready for other Behaviours or Strengths
A practised test and a plan for managing the time in each section

items.title: L13: Too junior, too vague, or about the team: senior diagnosis
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: At senior grades three faults recur, and a candidate can diagnose them in a draft. The first is evidence that is too junior: the example shows completion of tasks, support to a manager, or work inside one team, with no decisions or consequences beyond it. The test is to ask what the candidate decided and who was affected. The second is evidence that is too vague: the draft uses abstractions such as 'drove', 'enabled' or 'transformed' without naming what happened, how many people, over what time or with what result. The test is to ask whether a reader could repeat the story. The third is evidence about the team rather than the person: the draft says 'we' throughout, or credits the department's achievement without isolating the candidate's own action. The test is to ask whether each paragraph contains a decision or action that only the candidate took. At Grade 7 there is a fourth fault: the example is large and impressive but the candidate's role was supervisory in a thin way, so that decisions were taken by others while the candidate chaired or reported. The test is to ask whether the outcome would have differed if someone else were in the role. To repair a draft, begin with the choice of example: a better-fitting example fixes more than rewriting. If the example is right, restructure so that the candidate's decisions come first and context is short. Add specific outcomes, with approximations if necessary. Remove generic phrases that could appear in anyone's application. Finally, test the draft by explaining it aloud to a colleague who does not know your area; if they cannot say what you did, assessors cannot either.

questions.prompt: What is the best test of whether evidence is pitched too junior?

options.text: How many words does the example use, compared with the limit in the advert?
Does the example include a figure showing its scale?
Is the example written in the first person singular throughout?
What did the candidate decide, and who was affected?

questions.prompt: What is the best test of whether evidence is too vague to score?

options.text: Is the vocabulary formal enough for a senior post?
Could a reader repeat the story from what is written?
Does the example avoid acronyms and technical terms?
Is the example longer than 200 words, the usual length of a good one?

questions.prompt: Which test identifies evidence about the team rather than the person?

options.text: Does the statement mention team members by name or role?
Does each paragraph contain a decision or action only the candidate took?
Is the word 'we' completely absent from the statement?
Does the statement name a specific project or programme?

questions.prompt: What is the extra fault at Grade 7 described in the passage?

options.text: A large, impressive example where the candidate's role was thinly supervisory
An example that is too small to show any scope, however well it is described
An example with too many numbers, so that the actions get lost among the data
An example written in the first person where the third person is the norm at this grade

questions.prompt: Which question tests a thin-role example?

options.text: Would the outcome have differed if someone else were in the role?
Was the project completed on time and to the required standard?
Did the candidate attend the board and present the results?
Was the project large in budget and headcount terms?

questions.prompt: What is often the best first repair for a weak draft?

options.text: Rewrite every sentence in the draft using stronger verbs
Add more adjectives and adverbs to show how important the work was
Choose a better-fitting example
Shorten the first paragraph and add a summary of the Behaviours at the end

questions.prompt: If the example is right, how should a draft be restructured?

options.text: Describe the full history of the area first, then the decisions the candidate took
Describe the team's work first, then say what the candidate did within it
Give the results first, then list the actions only in a final short sentence
Put the candidate's decisions first and keep context short

questions.prompt: How can outcomes be handled when exact figures are unavailable?

options.text: Leave out outcomes that cannot be given as exact figures, to avoid being challenged
Use the team's figures as they stand, even where the candidate's own part is unclear
Describe the outcome as strong and successful without giving any detail of it
Add specific outcomes with honest approximations

questions.prompt: Why explain a draft aloud to a colleague outside your area?

options.text: To practise delivery speed and see whether the answer fits in the time allowed
To check the spelling and grammar of the statement before it is sent
If they cannot say what you did, assessors cannot either
To reduce the word count by removing details that the colleague already understands

questions.prompt: Which phrase is most likely to be generic filler?

options.text: I drove transformation across the area
I cut the average wait from ten days to six
I decided to stop the pilot
I told the board that the delivery date would slip
